title: The Return of the Beaver
context:
For roughly four hundred years, the beaver was missing from most of Europe. Hunters prized its dense fur, and also its castoreum, an oily secretion that was used in medicine and perfume, and by the early twentieth century only a few isolated groups survived in a handful of countries. Since the 1990s, however, a series of reintroduction projects has returned the animal to dozens of river systems, and the European population is now counted in the hundreds of thousands. Conservation bodies in several countries monitor the new colonies carefully, counting lodges each year and recording where the animals spread, because the speed of their recovery has surprised even the original supporters of the projects.

Beavers are often described as ecosystem engineers, because few animals alter their surroundings so deeply. They fell trees with their teeth and use the branches, mixed with mud and stones, to build dams across streams. Behind each dam a pond forms, and the extra water spreads gradually into the neighbouring soil. Not everyone welcomes the result. Farmers have reported flooded pasture and orchards stripped of young trees, and in one Scottish valley a single dam is said to have put two hectares of grazing land under water.

Scientific monitoring, however, points to unexpected benefits. In a five-year study in the south-west of England, researchers measured the flow of a stream before and after a family of beavers settled there. The dams slowed the movement of water during storms, so that the peak of each flood was reduced by about a third, and a village downstream that had flooded regularly stayed dry. Hydrologists nevertheless warn against overstating the case. When the ground is already saturated, beaver ponds fill to the brim and can do little to hold back a major flood.

Water quality also seems to improve. The still water in a pond allows sediment to settle, and with it much of the nitrogen and phosphorus that wash off fields treated with fertiliser, so the stream below runs clearer. Wildlife responds quickly: dragonflies, frogs and wetland birds are more numerous around beaver ponds, and in dry summers trout shelter in the deeper pools. Early fears that dams would block migrating salmon have largely proved unfounded. In most conditions the fish are able to leap or swim around the obstruction, although in very low water some are delayed for several days.

The practical challenge, therefore, lies less in ecology than in human tolerance. Compensation schemes can reimburse landowners, but money does not solve every dispute, and engineers have developed cheaper alternatives. A pipe passed through a dam can keep the pond at a fixed level, while wire mesh wrapped around the trunks protects individual trees. Only when such measures fail do authorities grant licences to remove the animals. Experience in Germany and Poland, where beavers have been present for decades, suggests that coexistence is possible provided advice is offered early, before a small problem becomes a feud.

The beaver, then, is neither the villain described by its critics nor the miracle worker promised by some enthusiasts. It is a powerful animal whose effects depend on where it settles, and the sensible approach is to decide in advance which places can accommodate it and which cannot. Such planning is already routine for other protected species, and there is no reason why it should not become routine for this one.
